list.listitem: Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) are autoimmune inflammatory myopathies associated with symmetric proximal muscle weakness, and can be associated with cutaneous findings (specifically DM), elevated muscle enzymes, findings of myopathy on electromyogram (EMG), and inflammation on muscle biopsy. C
Treatment focus should be on improving muscle strength and mitigating long-term sequelae. B
Most patients respond to corticosteroids and corticosteroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, azathioprine, or cyclophosphamide. B
Recommended treatment for patients with severe interstitial lung disease (ILD) at presentation is cyclophosphamide. B
The 10-year survival rate is estimated at 84%. B

background.definition: Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) are a heterogeneous group of autoimmune disorders, subtypes of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs), characterized by progressive proximal skeletal muscle weakness and inflammation on muscle biopsy. DM, unlike PM, is associated with characteristic cutaneous manifestations. In some cases, muscle involvement is delayed or lacking.

list.listitem: Annual incidence rates vary by country, with estimates for the United States ranging from 1.1-1.7 per 100,000 for DM and 2.46-3.8 per 100,000 for PM;, incidence increases with age.
The estimated prevalence per 100,000 in the United States ranges from 5.9-13 for DM and 9.7-15.48 for PM.,,

DM has a bimodal distribution, and affects adults between the ages of 40 and 70 years, as well as children (eg, juvenile dermatomyositis or JDM). PM typically presents between the ages of 40 and 60 years and is rarely seen in children. Both affect women more than men (2:1).
Estimated incidence of JDM is 2.5-4.1 per million. Age of onset of JDM is on average age 6.7 in girls and 7.3 in boys, though younger children can be affected.
A systemic review of the literature from 2000-2020 found that the prevalence of interstitial lung disease (ILD) in patients with PM or DM was 41%, with a higher prevalence in Asia.
Rapidly progressive ILD has a prevalence of 8.9% among DM/PM patients and is associated with anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) positive dermatomyositis.
African Americans are also at greater risk (relative risk = 2.8).
There is no clear cause for myositis, but there seems to be a genetic and immunologic predisposition with infectious and environmental triggers.

Implicated infections: Coxsackie virus, influenza virus, retroviruses, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus; additional infections implicated include protozoa, astodes, nematodes, and Borrelia species. Typically, viral myositis resolves in less than 6 weeks, but in patients with DM or PM, symptoms persist for more than 6 weeks. An exception is HIV myopathy which is chronic and associated with PM.
Genetic-specific HLA subtypes: HLA DRB1-03 in whites and HLA DRB1-14 in Koreans.
Environmental: Ultraviolet radiation intensity increases risk for DM similar to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Immunologic: Various autoantibodies found in up to 60% of patients. It is still unclear whether such autoantibodies directly affect disease pathogenesis.

The clinical definition of DM and PM does not match the pathological differences. Skin manifestations in DM may not manifest until later in the course and therefore DM may be mistaken for PM unless a muscle biopsy is obtained.
DM: The mechanism is complement-mediated microangiopathy. The inflammatory infiltrate is secondary to ischemic phenomena.
PM: Muscle fibers are damaged by cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes.

Dermatomyositis (DM) and/or polymyositis (PM) should be considered in patients with progressive, symmetric, and proximal muscle weakness for more than 6 weeks, especially in those with a positive ANA test result. C

Diagnosis should be confirmed by elevated serum muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase, AST, and ALT), an EMG demonstrating myopathy, and specific muscle biopsy findings of inflammation (myositis in PM; vasculitis between the muscle cells in DM). C

Differential.Differential_Features: inclusion bodies seen only on electron microscopy; characterized by proximal and distal muscle weakness (groove sign on forearms), mild facial weakness not involving extraocular muscles, possible leukoencephalopathy, associated with autoimmune disease, peripheral neuropathy may occur; muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and amyloid deposition
PM/DM associated with other connective tissues disorders, such as systemic sclerosis, mixed connective dissues disease (MCTD), Sjögren’s syndrome, SLE and rheumatoid arthritis
upper motor neuron signs, EMG shows fasciculation potentials and neurogenic changes
fluctuating weakness with repeated/sustained exertion, involvement of extraocular muscles, EMG shows abnormal decrement in repetitive nerve stimulation, antibodies to acetylcholine
such as muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies, and myotonic diseases; myopathic EMG changes, elevated CK, muscle biopsy, and genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis

history of taking medication that can cause myopathy such as lipid-lowering drug, hydroxyurea, D-penicillamine, immune checkpoint inhibitors, laxatives, glucocorticoids; stopping drug may correct the muscle damage
metabolic/endocrine abnormalities and associated symptoms, muscle weakness, abnormal blood test results; correction of metabolic/endocrine abnormality may reverse myopathy
asymmetric proximal and distal myopathy associated with sensory deficits, hypo/areflexia; NCS show demyelination, no signs of myopathy on EMG, CK normal
absence of (or mild) muscle weakness, mild or no CK elevation, no activity on EMG, muscle biopsy shows scleroderma vasculopathy, fiber atrophy without destruction, perimysial fibrosis
ILD, myositis, and rash similar to SLE and DM but patients also have sclerodactaly and Raynaud's phenomenon

occurs in up to 30% of patients with DM/PM; myositis occurs more frequently with certain autoantibodies, such as anti-Jo-1 antibodies; constellation of symptoms include fever, acute onset, Raynaud's phenomenon, mechanic's hands, ILD, arthritis

(also known as dermatomyositis sine myositis) has dermatopathology of DM but not the myopathy; CADM-140 may be seen and may be specific for amyopathic DM; muscle weakness may not be seen for as long as 6 years after onset of disease
associated myopathy could mimic inflammatory myopathy, but usually lacks proximal muscle weakness; there is rarely any weakness, despite elevated muscle enzymes
associated with anti-p155 and anti-p155/p140 antibodies, but tests are not yet routinely available

list.listitem: Common symptoms include difficulty with motor tasks that require the use of proximal muscles (eg, combing hair, getting out of a chair, or climbing stairs), frequent falls, fatigue, malaise, weight loss, shortness of breath, and low-grade fever. Distal muscle involvement occurs late in the course.
Common physical findings include muscle weakness, muscle atrophy, and abnormal breath sounds from cardiac or pulmonary involvement.

Less common symptoms include dysphagia from involvement of oropharyngeal and esophageal muscles, myalgias (in approximately one third of patients with PM), arthralgias when the myopathy is associated with other connective tissue diseases, palpitations, syncope, and systemic signs of autoimmune disease.
Peripheral neuropathy typically does not occur in PM or DM but could be seen in inclusion body myositis associated with malignancy, which could mimic PM or DM.

Less common physical findings seen primarily in DM include heliotrope rash with eyelid edema (red or blue-purple and pruritic), Gottron papules over knuckles associated with scalp dermatitis, nailfold changes from periungual dilation of capillaries, skin calcinosis usually in children (JDM), and joint swelling in association with other connective tissue diseases. The Gottron's rash in DM may be confused with that of SLE but Gottron's papules occur over knuckles and the rash in SLE occurs between the knuckles.
Other uncommon physical findings are arrhythmias seen in PM and DM, and congestive heart failure from cardiomyopathy.
Patients with anti-MDA5+ DM may present with rapidly progressive ILD, with or without other features of DM (eg, skin rash, muscle weakness).
Malignancy (particularly carcinoma) is common in patients with DM (45%).

Mild disease is characterized by muscle strength equal to or greater than 4/5, with no life-threatening complications; severe disease is associated with severe muscle weakness, myocarditis, respiratory failure, severe dysphagia, and ILD.
See for the role of diagnostic studies in the evaluation of DM and PM.

Chest x-rays can be useful in initial screening for infiltrates, pneumonitis, and scarring. If the result is abnormal, further testing with high resolution CT scan may be beneficial. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is useful in determining the ratios of inflammatory T4 and T8 cells used to determine inflammation. Patients with asymptomatic ILD or mild decrease in lung volumes and diffusing capacity on pulmonary function tests (PFTs) should be observed with serial PFTs.
Suspect DM or PM in patients aged 40 to 70 years with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, and proximal symmetric muscle weakness that can be insidious and develop gradually over weeks to months.
Initial laboratory testing should include CK and ANA levels.

Order an EMG to exclude neurogenic disorders and a muscle biopsy to make a definitive diagnosis. After muscle biopsy confirmation, an evaluation for specific autoantibodies can help determine prognosis.
Treatment should be focused on improving strength and minimizing long-term sequelae.
Initial therapy with high-dose corticosteroids is usually recommended for several months, followed by slow tapering to the lowest effective dose, depending on response to therapy. C
Methotrexate or azathioprine are used as first-line immunosuppressive agents if the disease is not controlled with corticosteroids alone or if the disease is rapidly progressive. C

If the disease is still not controlled with maximum doses of methotrexate or azathioprine, intravenous gammaglobulin, B rituximab, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine A, chlorambucil, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil have all been suggested as alternatives. C
Recommended treatment for patients with severe interstitial lung disease (ILD) at presentation is cyclophosphamide; mycophenolate may be another option. B
Other biologic agents, cytokine modulators, and monoclonal antibodies have shown some promise in the management of resistant disease by reducing serum CK levels and improving muscle strength. C
Recommended adjunct therapies include sunscreen, osteoporosis prevention, minimizing aspiration risk in patients with esophageal dysmotility, and physical therapy in patients with muscle weakness. C

Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) vary in severity of disease, ranging from mild disease, which responds rapidly to therapy, to more severe progressive disease, which is unresponsive to all treatment modalities. Slowly progressive cases of DM and PM are less likely to respond to treatment.

Goals of treatment include improving muscle strength and minimizing long-term extramuscular complications The more severe the initial illness and the higher the CK level, the better the response to treatment. Treatment response should be evaluated every few weeks by testing different muscles, particularly proximal muscles such as quadriceps, hip flexors, deltoids, and neck flexors.

Patients who respond early to high-dose corticosteroids typically respond better to corticosteroid-sparing agents; however, evidence of benefit is limited. Failure to respond to glucocorticoids should lead to further evaluation for inclusion body myositis, muscular dystrophy, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid-induced myopathy, and malignancy-associated myopathy, especially if the disease is not confirmed by muscle biopsy.
If the diagnosis of DM or PM is confirmed by muscle biopsy and the patient fails glucocorticoid therapy, this is an indicator of poor prognosis.
Treatment of ILD in PM and DM is based on the severity of dyspnea and abnormalities on PFTs.

Immunosuppressive therapy is warranted in those patients with ILD, who have more severe or progressive disease. There are myositis-specific autoantibodies such as anti-Jo-1 and anti-MDA5 autoantibodies that are associated with lung disease and with more severe disease.

A Cochrane review found a small benefit for cyclophosphamide in patients with DM/PM-associated ILD in terms of improving dyspnea and lung function (ie, change in forced vital capacity or FVC), but found it comparable to mycophenolate. Other patient-oriented outcomes are uncertain for cyclophosphamide.
See for drug therapies used in the treatment of DM and PM.
Other procedures (eg, total body irradiation, plasmapheresis) are experimental.
Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been suggested for use in cases of severe myositis, but clinical trials are lacking.
Biphosphonates should be recommended for corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis; also consider calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

Consider proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers for patients with peptic ulcer disease who are being treated with corticosteroids and those with dysmotility. Also consider measures to reduce aspiration risk in patients with dysmotility.
Consider Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis for in patients with anti-MDA5+ DM due to high incidence and mortality in these patients.
Recommend sunscreen.
The benefits of strength and aerobic exercise training are unclear.
Patients with severe or refractory DM or PM not responsive to outpatient management should be hospitalized.

Complications requiring hospitalization include bacterial/viral infections, opportunistic infections, septicemia from bacterial or fungal agents, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy presenting with syncope, shortness of breath, severe weakness, and respiratory failure.
All patients with DM or PM should be followed up by a rheumatologist.
Long-term sequelae of untreated disease include chronic muscle weakness, ILD, myocarditis, severe dysphagia, and respiratory failure. C

Factors associated with poor outcome include advanced age; myositis not responsive to glucocorticoid therapy; delayed initiation of treatment for more than 6 months after the onset of symptoms; severe weakness at diagnosis; the presence of extramuscular disorders, such as dysphagia; respiratory muscle weakness; ILD; cardiac involvement; and associated malignancy. B
The 5-year survival rate ranged from 52% to 65% in studies completed between 1971 and 1985, and has improved to 75% to 95% in studies completed between 2001 and 2006. B
The 10-year survival rate is predicted at 84%. B

feature.caption: Diagnostic Studies in the Evaluation of Dermatomyositis (DM) and Polymyositis (PM).

tr.td: Creatine kinase (CK)
Initial testing to evaluate for DM/PM; most sensitive muscle-derived enzyme
If elevated, supports diagnosis; usually parallels disease activity but can be normal in active disease
ANA
Initial testing to evaluate for DM/PM
Positive in 60% of patients; may be higher but current commercially available kits do not always detect myositis-specific antibodies
Other labs: LDH aldolase, myoglobin, liver enzymes-AST/ALT
Secondary tests to evaluate for DM/PM
If elevated, supports diagnosis
Myositis-specificantibodies (antisynthetase antibodies)
Predict treatment response

Presence of Mi-2 antibodies in DM associated with mild disease, good response to treatment, andgood long-term prognosis. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies associated with incomplete treatmentresponse and worse long-term prognosis. Anti-SRP (signal recognition particle) antibodies associated in some patients with high serum CK levels, muscle weakness, and minimal inflammation on biopsy. Anti-PL 7 and anti-PL 12 antibodies, may be present in interstitial lung disease without myositis or be associated with underlying connective tissue disease, most commonly DM/PM
MRI
Locate muscle biopsy site; evaluate degree of inflammation in muscles
Muscle atrophy, fatty infiltration noted. Muscles with inflammatory edema show increased signal intensity on T2 weighted imaging. Fat-suppressed MRI more sensitive and specific
Ultrasound
Locate muscle biopsy site; evaluate degree of inflammation in muscles
Muscle atrophy, decreased muscle bulk noted. Increased echogenicity noted because of fatty infiltration. Use of ultrasound is not well validated
EMG
Exclude neurogenic disorders and confirms myopathy
Findings include early recruitment of motor unit potentials; short duration and low-amplitude polyphasic motor units on voluntary activation, spontaneous activity increased at rest
Muscle biopsy
Provides definitive diagnosis

PM-biopsy shows muscle fiber necrosis, scattered atrophy, regeneration of muscle fibers, endomysial inflammatory infiltrates. DM-perifascicular atrophy (50% of patients), perivascular and perimysial inflammatory infiltrates

feature.caption: Drug Therapies Used in the Management of Dermatomyositis and Polymyositis.

tr.td: Glucocorticoids
Oral 1mg /kg/day, maximum dose 80 mg/day. For pulse IV therapy 1000 mg/day for 3 days
Taper gradually to lowest effective dose for 9-12 months

More than 6 weeks of therapy can cause steroid-induced myopathy. Edema, hypertension, acne, adrenal insufficiency, hypokalemia and other electrolyte abnormalities, weight gain, peptic ulcer, aseptic necrosis, osteoporosis, tendon rupture, convulsions, cataracts
Methotrexate
7.5 mg once weekly, gradually increasing the dose, maximum dose 25 mg/week.Folic acid 1milligram daily should be given concurrently
Taper monthly for 6 months after achieve remission

May be started at the same time as glucocorticoids, especially in severely ill patients. Side effects: gastrointestinal symptoms, leukopenia, increased risk for infection, immunosuppression, stomatitis, hepatotoxicty, pneumonitis
Azathioprine
50 mg once daily, gradually increasing every 1-2 weeks, maximum dose 2.5 t-mg/kg/day
Taper monthly for 6 months after achieve remission

May be started at the same time as glucocorticoids, especially in severely ill patients. Side effects: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, liver toxicity, hair loss, diarrhea, immunosuppression, leukopenia, increased risk for infection, fatigue, joint pains
Resume high-dose glucocorticoid therapy and add corticosteroid-sparing agent
1 mg/kg/day
Taper gradually to lowest effective dose for at least 12 months
Maximize dose of azathioprine or methotrexate or if dose already maximized, change to alternate corticosteroid-sparing agent
Rituximab
1000 mg IV
Day 0 and day 14
Side effects: diarrhea, rash, joint/muscle pains, fever,chills, immunosuppression, leukopenia, risk for infection
Immunoglobulin
1 or 2 gram/kg/day IV alone or in combination with IV glucocorticoids
3 months, 16 weeks
Side effects: headache, dermatitis, pedal edema, aseptic meningitis, venous thrombosis, acute renal failure, anaphylactic/allergic reactions
Other agents: cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, biological agents-eculizumab, etanercept, infliximab
Other agents for resistant skin disease: topical tacrolimus, hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab
Initial therapy: glucocorticoids
1 mg /kg/day
Reduce dose after 30 days to 40 mg/day for 2 months, tapered gradually

For severe ILD associated with impending respiratory failure use high-dose IV glucocorticoids, followed by oral glucocorticoids. Add second agent (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide) to reduce effects of glucocorticoids or for more severe or progressive disease
Rapidly progressive, severe disease: cyclophosphamide
IV: 1-2 mg/kg/day IV monthly, given with mesna (bladder protection). Oral: usual dose 1-3 mg/kg/day po, adjusted based on response/toxicity, maximum dose 5 mg/kg/day
6-12 months, maximum 2 years because of bladder cancer/leukemia risk

This recommendation is based on limited open-label studies; large clinical trials are difficult because of toxicity of drug, rarity of disease, and severity of complications if disease not treated. Side effects: leukopenia, immunosuppression, increased risk for infection, diarrhea, weight loss, rash, hematuria, gastrointestinal bleeding, cough, hair loss, leukemia, bladder cancer
